job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Pedro Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents, my uncle's family and my grandfather in a big shared house in Pune. Mornings I do my prayers, then send applications and check my email for site-engineer vacancies. Afternoons I sit in my father's hardware and building-supply shop and learn the accounts. Evenings I study for a site-safety certificate and walk around the neighbourhood with my cousins.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what was your internship?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did civil engineering at the College of Engineering in Pune and got a good result. For eight weeks I was an intern at a residential tower site run by a builder called Shree Developers, helping the site engineer, Mr Kulkarni, with measurements and daily progress reports. They liked my reports, which I wrote with a bit of help from AI to polish the English. I owe a small education loan, I have about two months saved, and my family would help if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine, and I'd say the same to my friends: good engineers will always be needed, because buildings don't build themselves. I'd keep using AI tools for report writing, as I do now, but not for anything important. I'd say the market will sort out who is good and who isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my worry is the building market, not AI. Builders in Pune have slowed their new projects because of high interest rates, and the junior site jobs are fewer. If I don't find something by next year, I'd join my father's business, but I'd prefer to earn my own place first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to about twenty builders and consultancies a month and finish the site-safety certificate, which employers like. I'd ask Mr Kulkarni and two family friends who run firms for introductions. In the meantime I'd keep learning my father's accounts, so I'm useful at the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady. A little restless, because my cousins are all earning already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you prefer your own place before joining your father's business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want my father's customers to respect me for what I do, not who my father is. If I walk in as the owner's son with no experience, I'm just that. If I walk in after two years on a site, I'm an engineer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it cost the family if you did join the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of pride, maybe, because they spent a lot on my degree. But my father says a degree is never wasted, and he'd put me on the supply side for contractors. That's where an engineer actually helps.

I'd say the market will sort out who is good.
think: My worry is the **building market**, since high interest rates slowed Pune's new projects.
If nothing comes by next year I'd join my father's shop, but I'd like to earn my own place first.
do: Apply to about **twenty builders** and consultancies each month.
Finish the **site-safety certificate**, which employers like.
Learn my father's **accounts** so I'm useful at the shop.
feel: Mostly steady, a little **restless**, because my cousins are all earning already.

fieldNote: The family shop is a real fallback, which keeps his mood at uneasy.
His pride is about being a **real engineer** first, not the owner's son.
He uses AI for polishing reports but does not see it as his problem.

steps.text: Apply to twenty builders and consultancies each month
Finish the site-safety certificate
Learn the shop's accounts with my father
Ask Mr Kulkarni for two introductions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a strong change and people who adapt will do well. Planning, checking and buying are on the card, and that's a lot of what builders do. I'd tell my cousins that the old way of working won't be enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think software will take the drawings, the estimates and the progress reports first, which is exactly where juniors start. Site work stays human for a while, because dust, weather and workers need people. I'd use the tools more, but my edge is judgement on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using AI properly for estimates and quantity take-offs, and learn a standard drawing program like Revit. I'd aim for site roles where I'm walking the floor, and I'd also look at the family's supply business, where I could bring in an online ordering system. If a builder wants an engineer who can do both site and software, I'd say that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Focused. I like that I can do something about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would your father's shop need an online system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because contractors waste half a day driving to the shop to ask if steel is in stock. If they could see stock and order from their phone, we'd sell more and they'd save time. My father is cautious about it, but I think he'd try it if I ran it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if your father said no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show him a small test with five customers, because he respects numbers. If it doesn't work I'd drop it. I don't want a quarrel with my father over a tool.

I'd tell my cousins the old way of working won't be enough.

Build an **online ordering** system for my father's shop.

Steady adaptability shows: he adopts tools once he sees them work.

steps.text: Learn Revit and use AI for quantity take-offs
Apply for site engineer roles at builders
Set up phone ordering for five of the shop's contractors
Keep my father's accounts for the shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too fast, and the government must not just leave it to the market. I'd also say that families should stay together and share what they have. I'd talk about it with my uncle, who is a builder and understands people and money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried. If AI does nearly any thinking work within two years, the planning, the drawings and the estimates go, and builders will do more with fewer juniors. Robots take longer, and construction is physical, so site work gives me a few more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my energy into the family businesses: I'd join my father's shop and my uncle's construction work, and take over the ordering and site coordination. I'd cut my spending and put my savings into a fixed deposit. I'd also learn the trades, like how scaffolding or electrical work is done, since a person who knows the site has value.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd keep steady for my parents. In our house, nobody falls alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your father that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Papa, I'd like to work at the shop and with Uncle on the sites. He'd probably say you studied for four years and I'd say yes, and now I'll use it where it's needed. He'd put his hand on my shoulder, and that would be enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this feel like a defeat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not exactly. A bit like the army taking my first choice and giving me a different post. I'd be sad, but a family business is also a kind of security that a job isn't.

say: I'd say two years is **too fast** and the government shouldn't leave it to the market.
Families should stay together and share what they have.
think: Planning, drawings and estimates go first, so builders will do more with **fewer juniors**.
Construction is physical, so site work gives me a few more years.
do: Join my father's shop and my uncle's **construction work** and take over ordering and coordination.
Cut spending and move my savings into a **fixed deposit**.
Learn the **trades**, such as scaffolding and electrical work.
feel: Anxious, but I'd stay steady for my parents, because in our house **nobody falls alone**.
S2.quote: A family business is also a kind of security that a job isn't.
fieldNote: His fallback is concrete: the shop and his uncle's sites.
He frames the family business as **security**, not defeat, which comes from his traditional values.
Anxious rather than alarmed because his household has income and work for him.

steps.text: Join my father's shop and take over the ordering
Work with my uncle on his construction sites
Move my savings into a fixed deposit
Learn scaffolding and electrical work on site

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build something solid if you start now. I'd tell my cousins to learn a trade or run a small business, because both are harder to replace. I'd tell the government to leave businesses free but support training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm cautious but fairly optimistic. If I get a site job this year, I'd have about four years to become an engineer people trust. I'd also have my father's shop as a base, so I'm not alone if something goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a site engineer post with a builder, and use my weekends to help modernise my father's shop. I'd put a quarter of my pay into a fixed deposit and some into a mutual fund. I'd study part time for a project management qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. It feels like I can build on this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the government to do, and not do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fund training and apprenticeships, yes, and keep the rules simple for small firms. I wouldn't want handouts, because people feel better when they earn. Every family I know would rather have a shop than a ration card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change this plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw builders stop hiring site engineers altogether, I'd go full-time into the family business. I'd watch the building permits in Pune, because they're a good sign of what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a comfortable time to prepare, and anyone who works steadily will find a place. I'd say the family is the best safety net, and the community should keep helping those in need. I'd tell friends not to follow every trend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel good. In ten years I could be a senior project engineer or running my own contracting firm. AI will change a lot, but people will still need houses and roads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with a job at a good builder for three or four years, then set up my own small contracting firm with my uncle's backing. I'd use AI where it helps, like estimates and scheduling, but keep the site judgement myself. I'd save for a house and marry within a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit proud. I can see the road ahead of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your own firm look like in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Perhaps twelve people, a few trucks, and a good name for finishing on time. I'd hire young engineers and give them what Mr Kulkarni gave me, which is patience. I'd also keep it small, because big firms forget the workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interest rates, bad partners, a collapse in building. AI is just one more uncertainty. I'd keep a cash reserve and not borrow too much, like my grandfather taught us.

The family is the best safety net.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time and many families have no shop to fall back on. What would help is training funded early, builders who keep hiring juniors, and banks that lend sensibly to small firms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd miss. I'd miss walking a site in the morning when the concrete is wet and the crew is shouting jokes. If a machine does everything, I'd want somebody still standing there to see it with their own eyes.

headlineQuote: If a machine does everything, I'd want somebody still standing there to see it with their own eyes.
portrait: Pedro is a **civil engineering** graduate in Pune, living in a joint family house, with a good result and no offer yet.
His father runs a hardware and building-supply shop, and his uncle runs a construction business, so he has real **fallbacks**.
He uses AI now and then for reports and estimates and adopts tools once he sees them work.
His mood runs from uneasy at most scenarios to anxious at two years, and calm at ten.
He favours work over handouts, wants simple rules for small firms, and believes the family is the best safety net.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI case, because many families have no shop to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: Training funded early and builders who keep **hiring juniors**.
Banks that lend sensibly to small firms.
